books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage, A. Trade, Diplomacy, and the Expansion of American Influence

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the Adams-Onís Treaty, 1819: The United States gained Florida from Spain in a treaty negotiated by Secretary of State John Quincy Adams. Spain gave up Florida, the United States gave up any claim to Texas, and the two nations fixed the boundary between the Louisiana Territory and Spanish land to the west. Florida had become a concern because enslaved people escaping from Georgia found refuge there. General Andrew Jackson had invaded Florida during the First Seminole War (1817–1818) to attack Seminole villages, and an earlier British-built fort on the Apalachicola River, which had passed into the hands of fugitive slaves and Seminoles, was destroyed by American forces in 1816.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Adams-Onís Treaty, 1819, and the First Seminole War. Paraphrased, not quoted; public domain sources.

stem: Under the Adams-Onís Treaty, the United States

options.text: gained Florida and gave up its claim to Texas
gained Texas and gave up its claim to Florida
options.misconception: The reverse happened: Florida came in, Texas was given up.

options.text: bought Florida from Britain after the War of 1812
gained Florida in exchange for the Oregon Country
options.misconception: Oregon was settled with Britain in 1846, not with Spain.

rationales.A: The passage states the bargain plainly: Spain gave up Florida, and the United States gave up any claim to Texas.
rationales.B: The treaty runs the other way. The United States gained Florida and surrendered its claim to Texas.
rationales.C: Florida belonged to Spain. Britain had nothing to sell, and the treaty was negotiated with Spain.
rationales.D: The Oregon Country was settled with Britain in 1846, twenty-seven years later. It was not part of this treaty with Spain.
rationales.general:
1. Find the bargain. Spain gave up Florida, and the United States gave up any claim to Texas.
2. Check the direction. Florida comes to the United States; the Texas claim goes away.
3. Put it together. The treaty traded one claim for one territory, and Florida was what the United States gained.
Background: The treaty also fixed the boundary between Louisiana and Spanish land to the west.
Remember: when a treaty swaps claims, track which side gains the land and which side drops a claim.
